rows.title: The multiple nobody publishes
rows.body:
A sub-$10M EBITDA company trades near 5.5x. The same company inside a $100M platform trades near 10x.

That spread is the entire buy-and-build thesis. It is also not automatic.

The gradient, from GF Data's sponsored-deal series: sub-$10M TEV around 5.5x, $10–25M around 5.9x, $100–250M around 10.0x. Add-ons ran about 40% of tracked deals in 2024 and now command roughly a 0.3x premium over platform entries. (GF Data is a subscription product covering sponsored transactions only — it undercounts founder-direct deals, and the publisher sells the data. It is still the best longitudinal series at this size.) Axial's own lower-middle-market average printed 6.07x in 2025 against a 5.70x five-year mean — different universe, same slope.

Everyone quotes the gradient as if the markup is conferred at close. Buy at six, own at ten.

Here's what the gradient actually prices: what the larger platform HAS. Systems instead of habits. Management depth instead of one indispensable owner. Revenue that survives any single relationship. Financials a lender can audit without archaeology.

An add-on earns the platform multiple only when it becomes those things. And it becomes those things — or doesn't — in the eighteen months after the wire clears: in technician retention, in customers who were loyal to a person rather than a company, in add-backs that turn out not to recur.

The multiple you exit at is set by what you integrate, not what you sign.

For anyone who has sold a platform: how much of your exit multiple would you honestly attribute to integration quality, versus scale alone?

rows.title: Dead Deal Economics
rows.body:
Three years ago, deals died on financing. Now they die on findings.

Axial's dead-deal data (75 broken lower-middle-market transactions, member-reported — and Axial sells the channel it measures) puts diligence findings behind ~47% of post-LOI breaks in 2025. QoE discrepancies as the killer more than doubled in two years while financing breaks fell by half.

The carousel covers what a dead deal costs, how long each buyer type sits in exclusivity before walking, and the part that interests me most: the four findings that kill deals are the same four that wreck integrations when the deal closes anyway.

A finding you didn't price doesn't disappear at close. It moves to the integration budget.

Which finding killed your last dead deal — and could you have seen it at day 4?

The uncomfortable part: the findings were there before the LOI. Owner dependence. Customer concentration. Add-backs that don't survive scrutiny. A working capital peg built on the broker's normalization instead of actuals.

Three questions before the LOI, not after: Do the add-backs survive a QoE? Does revenue survive the owner's exit? Is the peg built on actuals?

rows.title: The funnel is arithmetic
rows.body:
The average searcher looks at 3,000 companies to buy one. The median investor reviews 80+ opportunities per investment.

Top-of-funnel isn't an effort problem. It's arithmetic.

IESE's international search fund study: the average searcher explored over 3,000 businesses, had real conversations with 159 owners, signed about four LOIs, and closed one. Stanford's data puts the first LOI around month seven. And in the Journal of Private Equity, Teten and Farmer found the median PE fund needed 3.1 investment-team members to close a single transaction in a year. (Teten runs a sourcing firm — the number serves his argument. It also matches the academic funnels, which is why I'll use it.)

Most teams answer this math with intensity. More outreach, more conferences, longer hours. Coverage barely moves — the median firm still sees a fraction of the deals inside its own box.

The expensive failure isn't the deal you never saw.

It's the one you did see. Ninety days of exclusivity, a $40K QoE, three site visits — mispriced, because funnel exhaustion had set in and the team needed something to close. Scarcity at the top of the funnel quietly becomes optimism at the bottom. That optimism is what you overpay with. And it's what integration inherits.

Capacity discipline beats intensity. The funnel is math; staff it like math.

For anyone running an add-on program: how many closed deals per sourcing seat did you actually get last year?

rows.title: The 2026 HVAC read
rows.body:
Every HVAC deal priced off trailing-twelve numbers right now is priced off a cost structure that no longer exists.

The A2L refrigerant transition is adding 10–40% to equipment. A2L-certified labor is up double digits. And 83% of HVAC businesses raised prices in the past year (Jobber's 2026 survey — Jobber sells to these contractors, and it's still the widest sample going).

The carousel is the full 2026 read: equipment, labor, pricing power, a projected record replacement year, and a deal market where PE add-on volume nearly doubled year over year while industrials M&A fell by a quarter.

The part that matters for anyone buying: the environment now pays a premium for the things that are hardest to build — service agreements, technician pipelines, pricing discipline — and it punishes the same three findings that were always the tell: construction concentration, customer concentration, owner dependence.

A cost shock doesn't hit the model at close. It hits the P&L you inherited, in month seven.

Are you underwriting the transition, or the trailing twelve?

pages.label: what the shocks reward

pages.label: what they disqualify

rows.body_deck:
Every HVAC thesis written in 2025 priced in four things. Three of them have since expired.

The refrigerant crisis is over — HARDI said so in October 2025. R-454B peaked above $900 a cylinder and now runs $449–499, falling. The tariff stack is gone: SCOTUS struck the IEEPA duties 6–3 in February, and residential HVAC Section 232 was cut from 25% to 15% in June. And the R-410A installation deadline the whole mandated-replacement case rested on was withdrawn by EPA on 27 July.

The one that did not ease is labor. About 40,100 HVAC openings a year through 2034, and no purchase order fixes it.

Meanwhile the price came down. Capstone puts HVAC services at 9.5x EV/EBITDA across 2024–YTD 2026 against 13.3x across 2021–23. Roughly four turns.

A correction I owe this feed, since it is the kind that matters. I had a figure staged for this post claiming PE add-ons had nearly doubled year over year, attributed to S&P. I could not stand it up at that source or any other. Capstone’s actual count is 38 add-ons against 36 — two deals — and sector volume is down 4.2%. I am not going to restate the number I could not verify, because a figure repeated in order to knock it down is still a figure being repeated. The booming-deal-market version of this post was wrong, and it is not the one I am posting.

What is actually happening is duller and more useful: platform formation has slowed, add-ons carry the volume, and the good metros are taken. The opening is where the platforms have not formed yet.

If you are underwriting HVAC right now — have you re-run the model without the deadline in it?

rows.title: 37 days
rows.body:
Family offices walk away from broken deals in 37 days. Private equity funds take 106.

The gap isn't discipline. It's bench.

Axial's dead-deal data (75 broken lower-middle-market transactions, self-reported by members — Axial sells the intermediated channel, so weigh accordingly) tracked days under exclusivity before a deal died. Corporates: 125. Independent sponsors: 129. PE funds: 106. Family offices: 37.

The flattering read is decisiveness — family offices know their box and don't linger.

Here's the read I believe after a decade inside a PE-backed platform: when a finding surfaces on day 30 — an add-back that won't survive the QoE, revenue that leans on the owner, a peg built on the broker's normalization — someone has to call it. Fatal, or fixable and priceable?

The average family office runs about 12 people across the entire office (UBS 2025 Global Family Office Report — a survey of UBS's own client base, which skews large; most offices run leaner). Very few carry a dedicated deal team. When nobody can underwrite the fix, the safe answer is always walk.

Sometimes walking is right. But a fixable deal killed on day 37 never shows up as a cost. There's no line item for it. It's the acquisition you didn't make — priced, planned, integrated — because the finding arrived and the bench didn't.

For the family offices doing direct deals: when a finding lands mid-exclusivity, who in your shop makes the fatal-versus-fixable call?

rows.title: There is no $10 trillion silver tsunami
rows.body:
There is no $10 trillion silver tsunami.

There are roughly 2.9 million employer firms with owners over 55 — and most of them will never transact.

The $10T, twelve-million-business headline gets built by bundling in non-employer sole proprietorships: businesses with no employees and, mostly, no transferable enterprise value. One succession report that repeats the big number also warns of 30–50% double-counting across its own inputs — and that report comes from a firm that sells deal sourcing, so the caveat costs them. Credit where due.

The defensible floor is Project Equity's count: about 2.9 million employer firms with 55-plus owners. Real. Large. Not ten trillion.

And the supply isn't a wave — it's a backlog. Gallup found 67% of owners 55+ intend to close outright or don't know what they'll do. Heirs want liquidity, not the business, so owners postpone. Meanwhile the genuinely good companies get bought early, often by platforms, and what remains skews owner-dependent.

Which is the actual point. The test that separates an investable founder business from a valueless one — does revenue survive the owner's exit — is the same test that decides whether the integration works after you buy it. Screening and integration are one question, asked at two different times.

The tailwind is real. The TAM is marketing. The edge is skepticism.

What's your fastest tell — before the QoE — that a founder-owned shop has value that actually transfers?

rows.title: What a corp dev function actually costs
rows.body:
Nobody publishes what an add-on program costs to run. So here's the sheet, assembled from what is public — with every source's commercial interest named, because most of these numbers come from someone selling something.

The person: $150–250K before carry. The data stack: routinely six figures. The ramp: first LOI around month seven in search data, and no clean published number for time-to-first-sourced-close — a gap worth knowing by name. The coverage all of it buys: the median firm sees about 17.6% of its own market's deal flow, per the one longitudinal series that exists (published by a firm that sells origination analytics).

And the line nobody budgets: dead deals. $25–50K of QoE per busted exclusivity, with ~47% of post-LOI breaks now driven by diligence findings.

The sheet's conclusion isn't "spend less." It's that the function is expensive whether or not it works — so the question is where the next dollar of finite attention produces a return. On most platforms I've seen, the starved end isn't the top of the funnel.

If you've built this function: what did your cost per closed add-on actually come out to?

pages.text: QoE at LMM sizes runs $25–50K per busted exclusivity, and ~47% of post-LOI breaks now come from diligence findings (Axial, member-reported). Dead deals aren't an accident in this budget. They're a recurring line item.

pages.label: the headcount reality
pages.text: As of the last public count, ~30% of PE firms had no dedicated BD professional at all (SPS, 2021 — dated, and the most recent figure there is; below the mid-market the share is almost certainly higher).

pages.label: what the sheet says
pages.text: The function is expensive whether or not it works. So the real question is allocation: where does the next dollar of your team's finite attention produce a return — another seat at the top of the funnel, or capacity at the point where the return actually gets captured, after the wire clears?

rows.body_deck:
Nobody publishes what an add-on program costs to run. So here is the sheet, assembled from what is public — with every source’s commercial interest named, because most of these numbers come from someone selling something.

The person: $150–250K before carry. The data stack: routinely six figures. The ramp: first LOI around month seven in search data, and no clean published number for time-to-first-sourced-close — a gap worth knowing by name. The coverage all of it buys: the median firm sees about 17.6% of its own market’s deal flow, per the one longitudinal series that exists (published by a firm that sells origination analytics).

And the line nobody budgets: dead deals. $25–50K of QoE per busted exclusivity, with ~47% of post-LOI breaks now driven by diligence findings.

One page in the carousel does the arithmetic — fully loaded cost divided by sourced closes, somewhere between $60K and $200K each. It is labeled illustrative on the page, because it is my arithmetic on published ranges and not a benchmark anybody has established. Redo it with your own numbers.

The sheet’s conclusion is not "spend less". It is that the function is expensive whether or not it works — so the question is where the next dollar of finite attention produces a return. On most platforms I have seen, the starved end is not the top of the funnel.

If you have built this function: what did your cost per closed add-on actually come out to?

rows.title: The line item nobody underwrites
rows.body:
There's a cost in every [TRADE] acquisition I have never once seen in a model.

Across [N] deals it ran [$X–$Y] per acquisition. Every time.

[RECEIPT: what the cost is — named plainly, one sentence.]

It never appears in the LOI model because [RECEIPT: why it's invisible pre-close — who normalizes it away, or what it hides inside].

It shows up in [RECEIPT: the month/place it surfaces — which P&L line, which quarter].

The first [K] times, we treated it as a one-off. By deal [M] we underwrote it as a standing line — and the deals penciled differently. Some stopped penciling at all. That was the point.

The model you sign is a forecast of the business you hope you bought. The integration budget is the business you actually bought. The gap between them has recurring residents, and this is the most reliable one I know.

What's the line item that surprised you on your last add-on?
rows.body_alt:
The strongest objection to hiring outside deal-sourcing help is correct.

Sourcing is a core competency. The relationships are the asset. You shouldn't hand that off.

The objections are well documented: loss of control over the front of the process. Incentives that can reward deal volume over deal quality. Strategy and criteria shared outside the building. And the academic finding that investors with large, dedicated in-house sourcing teams cluster in the top quartile (Teten and Farmer — and the lead author runs a sourcing firm, which makes his pro-in-house finding more credible, not less).

I've sat on the platform side. Every one of those objections held at least once.

Here's what the market has actually converged on — including the vendors, when you read them closely: hybrid. Keep principal relationships, thesis ownership, and the final call in-house. Buy capacity where capacity is the constraint — coverage, screening, the diligence grind, and the post-close work that never gets staffed.

Because that's the honest version of make-versus-buy. It was never "who finds the deal." It's "where does your team's finite attention produce a return" — and on most platforms I've seen, the starved function isn't origination. It's what happens after the wire clears.

If you run BD in-house at a platform or fund: what did you deliberately decide NOT to build internally — and has that call held up?
